blocks.explanation:
A square-root function: there is no single number to find; we must draw the graph.
We need its domain (allowed x), range (possible y), a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: radicand \(\ge 0\) gives the domain; choose x so the radicand is a perfect square; plot and join with a smooth curve.
steps:
Given: \(y = \sqrt{3x}\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: domain from \(3x \ge 0\); table with \(3x\) a perfect square; plot and join smoothly.

Domain
\[3x \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge 0\]
Domain \(= [0, \infty)\).
Why: the square root of a negative number is not a real number.

Range
\(\sqrt{3x} \ge 0\), and it grows without limit as \(x\) grows.
Range \(= [0, \infty)\).
Why: the symbol \(\sqrt{\ }\) always means the non-negative root.

Table (make \(3x = 0, 1, 4, 9, 36\))
\[x:\ 0,\ \tfrac{1}{3},\ \tfrac{4}{3},\ 3,\ 12\]
\[y:\ 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 6\]
Why: choosing \(3x\) as a perfect square makes every y-value a whole number, so the points are exact.

Intercepts
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = 0\]
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow 3x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0\]
The graph meets both axes only at the origin \((0, 0)\).
Why: on the y-axis \(x = 0\) and on the x-axis \(y = 0\).

Draw the graph
Plot \((0, 0),\ (\tfrac{1}{3}, 1),\ (\tfrac{4}{3}, 2),\ (3, 3),\ (12, 6)\) and join them. The curve starts at the origin, rises steeply at first and then flattens: half of a parabola lying on its side.
Since \(\sqrt{3x} = \sqrt{3}\,\sqrt{x}\), it is the graph of \(y = \sqrt{x}\) stretched vertically by \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\).
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = 3:\ y = \sqrt{9} = 3 \;\checkmark\]
\[x = 12:\ y = \sqrt{36} = 6 \;\checkmark\]
Why: substituting table values back confirms the points lie on the curve.
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: starts at \((0, 0)\) and rises to the right through \((3, 3)\) and \((12, 6)\); domain \([0, \infty)\), range \([0, \infty)\); the only intercept is the origin.

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = square root of 3x: a half-parabola on its side starting at the origin and rising through (1/3, 1), (4/3, 2), (3, 3) and (12, 6).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (i): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
A square-root function: there is no single number to find; we must draw the graph.
We need its domain (allowed x), range (possible y), a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: radicand \(\ge 0\) gives the domain; choose x so the radicand is a perfect square; plot and join with a smooth curve.
steps:
Given: \(y = \sqrt{x} + 5\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: domain from \(x \ge 0\); table with \(x\) a perfect square; plot and join smoothly.

Domain
\[x \ge 0\]
Domain \(= [0, \infty)\).
Why: the radicand is \(x\), which must not be negative.

Range
\[\sqrt{x} \ge 0 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x} + 5 \ge 5\]
Range \(= [5, \infty)\).
Why: adding 5 to a quantity that is at least 0 gives a quantity that is at least 5.

Table (\(x = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16\))
\[x:\ 0,\ 1,\ 4,\ 9,\ 16\]
\[y:\ 5,\ 6,\ 7,\ 8,\ 9\]
Why: perfect squares give whole-number roots.

Intercepts
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = 5\]
y-intercept \((0, 5)\).
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x} = -5\]
This is impossible, so there is no x-intercept.
Why: a square root is never negative, so the graph never reaches the x-axis.

Draw the graph
Plot \((0, 5),\ (1, 6),\ (4, 7),\ (9, 8),\ (16, 9)\) and join them. The curve starts at \((0, 5)\) and rises slowly to the right.
It is the graph of \(y = \sqrt{x}\) shifted 5 units up.
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = 9:\ y = 3 + 5 = 8 \;\checkmark\]
Every y-value in the table is at least 5, as the range says.
Why: the table agrees with the domain and range found earlier.
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: starts at \((0, 5)\) and rises slowly through \((4, 7)\) and \((16, 9)\); domain \([0, \infty)\), range \([5, \infty)\); y-intercept \((0, 5)\), no x-intercept.

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = square root of x plus 5: starts at (0, 5) and rises slowly through (1, 6), (4, 7), (9, 8) and (16, 9).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (ii): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
A square-root function: there is no single number to find; we must draw the graph.
We need its domain (allowed x), range (possible y), a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: radicand \(\ge 0\) gives the domain; choose x so the radicand is a perfect square; plot and join with a smooth curve.
steps:
Given: \(y = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{x}\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: domain from \(x \ge 0\); table with \(x\) a perfect square; plot and join smoothly.

Domain
\[x \ge 0\]
Domain \(= [0, \infty)\).
Why: the radicand \(x\) must not be negative.

Range
\[\sqrt{x} \ge 0 \Rightarrow -\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{x} \le 0\]
Range \(= (-\infty, 0]\).
Why: multiplying a non-negative number by a negative number \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives a number that is zero or negative.

Table (\(x = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16\))
\[x:\ 0,\ 1,\ 4,\ 9,\ 16\]
\[y:\ 0,\ -\tfrac{1}{2},\ -1,\ -\tfrac{3}{2},\ -2\]
Why: perfect squares give exact values; for example \(x = 9\): \(-\tfrac{1}{2}(3) = -\tfrac{3}{2}\).

Intercepts
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = 0\]
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x} = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0\]
The only intercept is the origin \((0, 0)\).
Why: both conditions lead to the same point.

Draw the graph
Plot \((0, 0),\ (1, -0.5),\ (4, -1),\ (9, -1.5),\ (16, -2)\) and join them. The curve starts at the origin and falls slowly to the right, below the x-axis.
It is \(y = \sqrt{x}\) reflected in the x-axis (the minus sign) and squashed to half its height (the factor \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)).
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = 16:\ y = -\tfrac{1}{2}(4) = -2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the value agrees with the table and lies in the range \((-\infty, 0]\).
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: starts at \((0, 0)\) and falls slowly through \((4, -1)\) and \((16, -2)\); domain \([0, \infty)\), range \((-\infty, 0]\); the only intercept is the origin.

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = minus one half times square root of x: starts at the origin and falls slowly through (1, -0.5), (4, -1), (9, -1.5) and (16, -2).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (iii): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
A square-root function: there is no single number to find; we must draw the graph.
We need its domain (allowed x), range (possible y), a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: radicand \(\ge 0\) gives the domain; choose x so the radicand is a perfect square; plot and join with a smooth curve.
steps:
Given: \(y = -\sqrt{x + 1} + 2\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: domain from \(x + 1 \ge 0\); table with \(x + 1\) a perfect square; plot and join smoothly.

Domain
\[x + 1 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge -1\]
Domain \(= [-1, \infty)\).
Why: the radicand \(x + 1\) must not be negative.

Range
\[\sqrt{x + 1} \ge 0 \Rightarrow -\sqrt{x + 1} \le 0\]
\[-\sqrt{x + 1} + 2 \le 2\]
Range \(= (-\infty, 2]\).
Why: the minus sign makes the root part zero or negative; adding 2 makes the whole at most 2.

Table (make \(x + 1 = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16\))
\[x:\ -1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 8,\ 15\]
\[y:\ 2,\ 1,\ 0,\ -1,\ -2\]
Why: perfect squares under the root give whole-number values, e.g. \(x = 8\): \(-\sqrt{9} + 2 = -1\).

Intercepts
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1 + 2 = 1\]
y-intercept \((0, 1)\).
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x + 1} = 2\]
\[x + 1 = 4 \Rightarrow x = 3\]
x-intercept \((3, 0)\).
Why: squaring both sides of \(\sqrt{x + 1} = 2\) removes the root; 2 is positive, so the solution is valid.

Draw the graph
Plot \((-1, 2),\ (0, 1),\ (3, 0),\ (8, -1),\ (15, -2)\) and join them. The curve starts at \((-1, 2)\) and falls to the right, crossing the x-axis at \((3, 0)\).
It is \(y = \sqrt{x}\) moved 1 unit left, reflected in the x-axis and moved 2 units up.
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = 3:\ y = -\sqrt{4} + 2 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
\[x = 15:\ y = -4 + 2 = -2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the intercept and a far point both satisfy the equation.
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: starts at \((-1, 2)\) and falls to the right through \((0, 1)\), \((3, 0)\) and \((15, -2)\); domain \([-1, \infty)\), range \((-\infty, 2]\); y-intercept \((0, 1)\), x-intercept \((3, 0)\).

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = minus square root of (x + 1) plus 2: starts at (-1, 2) and falls through (0, 1), (3, 0), (8, -1) and (15, -2).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (iv): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
A cube-root function: we must draw its graph.
We need its domain, range, a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: a cube root exists for every real number, so the domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}\); choose x so the radicand is a perfect cube; plot and join smoothly.
steps:
Given: \(y = \sqrt[3]{2x + 1}\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: every real number has a real cube root; table with \(2x + 1\) a perfect cube; plot and join smoothly.

Domain
\(2x + 1\) can be any real number.
Domain \(= \mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\).
Why: a cube root of a negative number is negative, e.g. \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\), so no x-value is excluded.

Range
Range \(= \mathbb{R}\).
Why: \(2x + 1\) takes every real value, and so does its cube root.

Table (make \(2x + 1 = -8, -1, 0, 1, 8, 27\))
\[x:\ -\tfrac{9}{2},\ -1,\ -\tfrac{1}{2},\ 0,\ \tfrac{7}{2},\ 13\]
\[y:\ -2,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3\]
Why: solving \(2x + 1 = k\) gives \(x = \tfrac{k - 1}{2}\); perfect cubes \(k\) give whole-number y-values.

Intercepts
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt[3]{1} = 1\]
y-intercept \((0, 1)\).
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow 2x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\]
x-intercept \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, 0)\).
Why: a cube root is 0 only when the number inside is 0.

Draw the graph
Plot the six points and join them. The curve is an S-shape rising from left to right, almost vertical near \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, 0)\) and flattening on both sides.
It is \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\) moved \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) unit left and squeezed horizontally by the factor 2; its centre is \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, 0)\).
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = 13:\ y = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3 \;\checkmark\]
\[x = -\tfrac{9}{2}:\ y = \sqrt[3]{-8} = -2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: one point on each side of the centre agrees with the table.
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: a rising S-shaped curve centred at \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, 0)\) through \((-\tfrac{9}{2}, -2)\), \((0, 1)\) and \((13, 3)\); domain and range \(\mathbb{R}\); intercepts \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\).

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = cube root of (2x + 1): a rising S-shaped curve through (-9/2, -2), (-1, -1), (-1/2, 0), (0, 1), (7/2, 2) and (13, 3).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (v): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
A cube-root function: we must draw its graph.
We need its domain, range, a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: a cube root exists for every real number, so the domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}\); choose x so the radicand is a perfect cube; plot and join smoothly.
steps:
Given: \(y = 2\sqrt[3]{x} - 3\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: table with \(x\) a perfect cube; plot and join smoothly.

Domain and range
Domain \(= \mathbb{R}\), range \(= \mathbb{R}\).
Why: \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) exists for every real \(x\) and takes every real value; doubling and subtracting 3 keeps that true.

Intercepts
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = -3\]
y-intercept \((0, -3)\).
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow \sqrt[3]{x} = \tfrac{3}{2}\]
\[x = \left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{27}{8}\]
x-intercept \((\tfrac{27}{8}, 0)\), about \((3.4, 0)\).
Why: cubing both sides removes the cube root.

Draw the graph
Plot \((-8, -7),\ (-1, -5),\ (0, -3),\ (1, -1),\ (8, 1),\ (27, 3)\) and \((\tfrac{27}{8}, 0)\), and join them. The S-shaped curve rises from left to right, steepest at \((0, -3)\).
It is \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\) stretched vertically by 2 and moved 3 units down; its centre is \((0, -3)\).
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = \tfrac{27}{8}:\ y = 2\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right) - 3 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
\[x = 27:\ y = 2(3) - 3 = 3 \;\checkmark\]
Why: the x-intercept and a table point both satisfy the equation.
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: a rising S-shaped curve centred at \((0, -3)\) through \((-8, -7)\), \((1, -1)\), \((8, 1)\) and \((27, 3)\); domain and range \(\mathbb{R}\); intercepts \((0, -3)\) and \((\tfrac{27}{8}, 0)\).

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = 2 times cube root of x minus 3: a rising S-shaped curve through (-8, -7), (-1, -5), (0, -3), (1, -1), (27/8, 0), (8, 1) and (27, 3).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (vi): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
A cube-root function: we must draw its graph.
We need its domain, range, a table of exact points and the intercepts.
Plan: a cube root exists for every real number, so the domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}\); choose x so the radicand is a perfect cube; plot and join smoothly.
steps:
Given: \(y = \sqrt[3]{x^2 + x - 2}\).
To find: its graph (with domain, range and intercepts).
Method: study the quadratic inside the root (its zeros and least value), then tabulate, plot and join smoothly.

Study the radicand
\[x^2 + x - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1)\]
\[\text{least value at } x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\]
\[\tfrac{1}{4} - \tfrac{1}{2} - 2 = -\tfrac{9}{4}\]
Why: the radicand is an upward parabola with zeros \(-2\) and 1 and vertex \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{9}{4})\); the graph is symmetric about \(x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Domain and range
Domain \(= \mathbb{R}\).
\[x^2 + x - 2 \ge -\tfrac{9}{4} \Rightarrow y \ge \sqrt[3]{-\tfrac{9}{4}}\]
Range \(= \left[-\sqrt[3]{\tfrac{9}{4}},\ \infty\right)\), where \(\sqrt[3]{\tfrac{9}{4}} \approx 1.31\).
Why: the cube root keeps order (a bigger number has a bigger cube root), so the least radicand gives the least y.

Intercepts
\[y = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 2)(x - 1) = 0\]
x-intercepts \((-2, 0)\) and \((1, 0)\).
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt[3]{-2} \approx -1.26\]
y-intercept \((0, -\sqrt[3]{2})\).
Why: a cube root is zero exactly when the radicand is zero.

Draw the graph
Plot the points and join them smoothly. The curve comes down from the upper left, turns sharply (almost vertically) at \((-2, 0)\), has a rounded bottom at \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, -1.31)\), turns sharply up again at \((1, 0)\) and rises to the upper right.
Its shape is a wide 'U' with a flat bottom, symmetric about the line \(x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\).
Why: the points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight pieces, because the function changes smoothly between the plotted points.

Check
\[x = 2:\ \sqrt[3]{4} \text{ and } x = -3:\ \sqrt[3]{9 - 3 - 2} = \sqrt[3]{4}\]
Why: points equally far from \(x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\) (here 2 and \(-3\)) give the same y, confirming the symmetry.
blocks.final_answer: Graph drawn: a wide U-shaped curve, symmetric about \(x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\), with lowest point \((-\tfrac{1}{2}, -\sqrt[3]{9/4}) \approx (-0.5, -1.31)\), crossing the x-axis steeply at \((-2, 0)\) and \((1, 0)\) and the y-axis at \((0, -\sqrt[3]{2})\); domain \(\mathbb{R}\), range \(\left[-\sqrt[3]{9/4},\ \infty\right)\).

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = cube root of (x squared + x - 2): a wide U-shape symmetric about x = -1/2, lowest point about (-0.5, -1.31), crossing the x-axis steeply at (-2, 0) and (1, 0).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (vii): the graph with its table points and intercepts (original drawing)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (book page 295) shows eight graphs, labelled (i) to (viii), for this question, but only seven parts are printed. Graphs (i) to (vii) match the printed parts; graph (viii) (another S-shaped cube-root curve) belongs to no printed part and should be ignored.
